claims.claim: A health system consists of all the organizations, people, and resources whose primary purpose is to promote, restore, or maintain health, and every health system performs the functions of financing, service delivery, resource generation, and governance/stewardship.

The WHO framework for action (2007) describes health systems through six building blocks: service delivery; health workforce; information; medical products, vaccines and technologies; financing; and leadership/governance.
US national health expenditure reached $5.3 trillion in 2024, growing 7.2 percent and accounting for 18.0 percent of GDP (up from 17.7 percent in 2023).

In 2024, US health spending by major source of funds was: private health insurance 31 percent (about $1.6 trillion), Medicare 21 percent (about $1.1 trillion), Medicaid 18 percent ($931.7 billion), and out-of-pocket 11 percent ($556.6 billion) — evidence that the US is a mixed, multi-payer system.

By type of sponsor in 2024, the entities ultimately financing US health care were the federal government (31 percent), households (28 percent), private businesses (18 percent), and state and local government (16 percent).

The US uninsured rate was 8.2 percent in 2024 (American Community Survey), a statistically significant increase from 7.9 percent in 2023; CMS reported the insured share of the population at 91.8 percent in 2024.

Health systems are commonly grouped into models: the Beveridge (tax-funded, government-provided), Bismarck (employment-based social insurance, multiple non-profit funds), national health insurance (private provision paid by a single government insurer), and out-of-pocket models; T.R. Reid argues the US uniquely uses all four across different populations.

Medicare is a federal program (66.6 million enrollees in 2024) and Medicaid is a joint federal-state program (84.3 million beneficiaries in 2024), which is why US public coverage varies rather than forming one uniform national system.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The 2024 uninsured rate differs slightly by survey.
positions: Census American Community Survey: 8.2 percent uninsured in 2024
Census Current Population Survey: 8.0 percent uninsured in 2024
CMS NHE: insured share 91.8 percent (implies about 8.2 percent uninsured)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: All three are close and consistent to within survey error; the lesson cites the ACS 8.2 percent figure and names the survey and year, noting different surveys yield slightly different estimates.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only generic boilerplate ('a foundational concept... introduces its meaning, its context, and a simple way to apply it') with no substantive claims about health systems; none of it was usable.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate definition with a sourced definition of a health system and its core functions.
Added dated, sourced US financing figures (2024 CMS NHE) in place of the draft's contentless prose.

rightsIssues: CMS, WHO, and Census materials are cited as authoritative references; all prose is original synthesis. WHO's 'Everybody's business' framework text was read via a peer-reviewed secondary (PMC5651704) because the WHO IRIS PDF is JavaScript-gated; the canonical WHO handle is registered as the source URL.

The four-models framing (PNHP page) is authored by journalist T.R. Reid; it is REFERENCE_ONLY secondary and is used only for the model taxonomy and the interpretive point that the US uses all four models.

sourceRecords.title: Everybody's business: strengthening health systems to improve health outcomes — WHO's framework for action
sourceRecords.notes: Canonical WHO 2007 framework defining the six health-system building blocks (service delivery; health workforce; information; medical products, vaccines and technologies; financing; leadership/governance) and system goals. The IRIS PDF is JavaScript-gated; the building-block names and citation were confirmed via the peer-reviewed article PMC5651704, which reproduces them. Facts synthesized in original wording; no framework text reproduced.
